turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Doctor. They're in room two. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-two.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): He says the headache is already there this morning. I didn't take a temperature.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Come in, both of you, sit, sit. I'm glad you battled through the traffic to get here.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me, in your own words, what's been happening.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Um. I don't know, doctor. The headaches have been with me for years, maybe five, maybe longer, but it's different now. Mornings are the worst.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Shame, he's really not himself. The morning ones have been this bad for about three weeks. He snores like a tractor all night, and then he's half asleep at work.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, I don't snore. And I'm not tired. She worries too much. The head just wakes me, that's all.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. How has the morning pain been feeling, when it's there?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): I get sick with it. Properly sick, not just a bit off.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sick as in you've actually vomited?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja. Not every morning. A few times. I don't know when that started, doctor, I really don't.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): And the bad mornings are longer than three weeks. Heavy, right behind the eyes. It was already like that before we went to the coast. Two months? I don't know.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm telling you, three weeks. He only started going on about it after my sister's birthday.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll hold both versions for now. The older headaches, over the years, did someone call those migraines?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Ja, the other doctor said migraine. The light bothers me and I have to lie in a dark room. These morning ones aren't quite the same.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): And day to day, how has this been sitting with you?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): The load shedding is what's getting me, hey. The neighbour's generator runs half the night and the bakkie deliveries are all behind.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): How often are you taking something for the pain?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Two Panados. They take the edge off, then by lunch it's sitting there again.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Most days, or only now and then?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Most mornings. Two tablets. Not twice a day, if she's been saying that she's exaggerating.
[SEG0022] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does take another two after work. And those white tablets in the green box from the chemist, I don't even know the name.

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): That's the Imigran. I don't take that every day, only for the old migraine. The strength, I think it's fifty milligrams, or maybe a hundred. I don't know, doctor, the box is at home.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you take the Imigran the way it was intended, right when the attack starts?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I forget, and then I take it late.
[SEG0026] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And when the Panado runs out he uses Grandpa powders. I saw that last week.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you using the Grandpa as well?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Only if the Panado's finished. Once last week, I think. I don't know.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever with all of this?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No fever.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fits, or blackouts, even a short one?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I would remember.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about weakness, or numbness, in the arms or the legs?
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Work's been hectic, doctor. I don't even know if the boss believes I'm sick, with all the deliveries piling up.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm, we'll leave work there. Any blurring, or seeing double?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I won't push the eye question. I'm just going to have a quick look at the nerves.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Follow my finger. Pupils are equal, and they both react to light. There's no droop of the face.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Squeeze my fingers. Power is good in both hands. Push the legs up against my hand. Strong, both sides.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Now touch your nose, then my finger. That's smooth. Your neck isn't stiff.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Is it bad, doctor? I don't know what you're finding.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm just checking. Nothing on the examination is worrying me.
[SEG0043] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): But the snoring, and him being tired all day, you're leaving that?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm not tired. I told you. The head wakes me, I get up, I drive. That's the whole story.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I hear both of you. Snoring and sleepiness can matter, but you don't feel tired, so I'm not going to hang a label on it today.

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): My working thought is that the old migraine may be changing its pattern. Morning pain with vomiting can also mean a pressure problem, and I can't rule that out from this visit.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): A pressure problem? I don't know, doctor. Like a tumour?
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying a tumour. Most of this still sits with migraine, but this new morning pattern deserves respect.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the Imigran for a clear migraine attack only, not as a morning tablet. And ease off the Panado every day, because a daily habit can feed the headache.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): So I just stop? I don't know if I can do the mornings without them.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not cold turkey. Use them when it's truly sore, not automatically with the coffee. And the Grandpa counts as the same pain medicine, not a free extra.
[SEG0052] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What about a scan? I told him ages ago we should ask.
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the early-morning headache and the vomiting are still there when I see you again, I'll arrange a CT scan of the head. Not today. Only if it hasn't settled.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks either way. If you get a sudden worst headache of your life, weakness, or you can't stay awake, go straight to casualty and don't wait for me.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay. I don't know if it'll be gone by then, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to lean in. Must I book that two-week visit?
[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes please, two weeks, and no scan form for now.
[SEG0058] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put it in the book before you go. We'll leave the blood pressure as it is.
[SEG0059] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. I'll make sure he pitches up, even if he says he's fine.
[SEG0060] person_3 (PATIENT): Ag, I'll come. I just hope it's nothing. That generator was going again last night, but that's another story.

spec.situation: Person with long headaches who now has a different pattern (worse in the morning, or with vomiting); takes sumatriptan or paracetamol often; partner says snoring and tiredness too; patient dismisses it. Doctor does a quick neuro exam and orders a scan conditionally.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Vomiting a few times, not every morning is stated; certainty is not uncertain because patient clearly confirms vomiting.
bad.text: vomiting (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, frequency=a few times, not every morning, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Light sensitivity is stated for old migraine; current temporality isn't supported for present complaint.
bad.text: light sensitivity (category=ophthalmological, status=present, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Temperature was not taken by the nurse.
The patient reported that the longstanding headaches had previously been diagnosed as migraine by another doctor.
Panado use detail: the patient said the two tablets 'take the edge off' but by lunch the headache is back.
The patient gave an uncertain answer to visual symptoms: 'sometimes, not really' when asked about blurring or double vision; this possible visual disturbance/uncertainty is not recorded.
Negative finding omitted: no weakness or numbness in the arms or legs was not established because the patient did not answer the question; this should not be implied as assessed/negative.
Doctor stated that nothing on the examination was worrying.
The doctor considered snoring and sleepiness potentially relevant but did not diagnose it because the patient denied feeling tired.
Plan detail omitted: the doctor advised not to stop analgesics 'cold turkey' and to use them only when the headache is truly sore, not automatically with coffee.
Conditional CT plan detail: the doctor explicitly said 'not today' regarding the head CT, and later confirmed 'no scan form for now.'
